title: Family-centred care, partnership with parents and family cultures
blurb: Plan care in partnership with parents and the wider family, respect different family structures and cultures, and keep the child at the centre.
question: A 2-year-old is admitted for nasogastric feeding. His mother wants to give the feeds herself and stay overnight, and the family follow a halal diet. How should the nurse plan care in partnership with the family?

teach.h: The family is the constant in a child's life
teach.body: Family-centred care plans and delivers children's care in partnership with the family, recognising parents and carers as the child's principal caregivers and advocates, while keeping the child's own voice and welfare central. Plain English: parents are partners, not visitors, and each family decides with you how involved they want to be.
teach.cite: NICE NG204 Babies, children and young people's experience of healthcare (2021) 1.5.1

teach.h: What NICE NG204 says the environment should support
head: Support
Example

teach.body: Some parents want to do all their child's care; others need a break, have other children or work shifts. Agree with each family what they would like to do, teach and support them, and review it. Never judge a parent's commitment by how long they stay. Children and young people should also be asked how involved they want their parents to be.

steps.label: Ask
steps.sub: What would you like to do? What is usual at home?

steps.label: Agree
steps.sub: Who does which care; record it

teach.note: Ask, do not assume. Forms and language should fit the family in front of you.

rows.label: Under-16s
values: Not acceptable except in an emergency

teach.caption: NHS England, Guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services in primary care (2018).

items: Mila, 2, is admitted for nasogastric feeding. Her mother, Joanna, wants to give the feeds and stay overnight; the family eat halal food.
Nurse Sam asks about Mila's routines, comforters and words she uses, and agrees with Joanna which care she will do.
Sam teaches and supervises Joanna's NG feeds, including checking tube position, until she is confident and competent, and records the agreement.
Sam arranges a parent bed, orders halal meals and asks whether Mila's older brother would like sibling support from the play team.

teach.text: Family-centred is not parent-centred. The child's welfare and voice stay central: if a parent's wishes conflict with the child's safety, the child comes first. And partnership does not mean handing over care without teaching and checking competence.

items: Parents are the principal caregivers and advocates of babies and young children (NG204 1.5.1).
Agree with each family what care they want to give; teach, support and review.
Support parents to stay, siblings to visit, and cultural, dietary and faith needs.
Use professional interpreters; do not use children to interpret.
Respect diverse family structures; check who holds parental responsibility.

summary: You can now plan care in partnership with families, negotiate parental participation, meet cultural, dietary and faith needs, use professional interpreters and respect diverse family structures, while keeping the child's welfare at the centre.

A.q: In family-centred care, how should a parent's participation in their child's hospital care be decided?
options: Agreed with the parent and reviewed as needs change
Set by the nurse in charge for all families on the ward
Parents carry out all care the child usually has at home
Parents observe while nurses deliver all hands-on care
A.why: Participation is negotiated with each family according to their wishes and abilities, with teaching and support, and reviewed over time (NG204).

whyNot.1: A fixed ward rule ignores each family's circumstances.
whyNot.2: Expecting parents to do everything may overwhelm them; it should be their choice.
whyNot.3: Excluding parents from care they want to give is not partnership.

A.q: Bilal, 3, is admitted with pneumonia. His mother speaks little English and his 11-year-old sister offers to interpret. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the sister's offer as she knows the family
Use gestures and written English until the father arrives
Arrange a professional interpreter for the conversation
Ask a bilingual parent on the ward to help
A.why: A professional interpreter ensures accurate, confidential communication; children should not be used as interpreters except in an emergency.

whyNot.0: Using an 11-year-old to interpret is not acceptable outside an emergency.
whyNot.1: This delays informed communication and risks misunderstanding.
whyNot.3: Another parent is untrained and breaches confidentiality.

A.q: Zara, 6, is admitted for a week. Her parents work shifts and cannot stay overnight. A colleague comments that 'good parents stay'. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Agree, and document the parents' absence
Report the parents' absence to the safeguarding lead
Ask the parents to arrange unpaid leave from work
Respect their circumstances and plan contact
A.why: Family-centred care respects each family's circumstances; the nurse should agree how the family will stay involved (calls, visits) rather than judge them.

whyNot.0: This reinforces a judgement that is not based on the child's welfare.
whyNot.1: Not staying overnight is not on its own a safeguarding concern.
whyNot.2: Pressuring parents about work is not appropriate; involvement can be arranged in other ways.

B.q: Jack, 4, is admitted with two adults who introduce themselves as his mums. The admission form has fields for 'mother' and 'father'. What should the nurse do?
options: Record one as mother and leave father blank
Record both as parents using the family's terms
Ask which of them is the 'real' mother
Record the birth mother and list the other as a visitor
B.why: Respecting family structures means using the family's own terms. Parental responsibility can be held by a second female parent, so check PR as for any family without making assumptions.

whyNot.0: This leaves an inaccurate record of who his parents are.
whyNot.2: This is disrespectful and irrelevant to his care.
whyNot.3: This assumes a status and may exclude a parent with parental responsibility.

B.q: Aaron, 5, has been in hospital for a week. His father has stayed every night and says he feels he has to do all Aaron's care. What is the best response?
options: Thank him and leave the care arrangements as they are
Advise him to go home so nurses can take over
Tell him this is expected of parents on the ward
Review together what he wants to do and offer support
B.why: Participation is negotiated and reviewed; parents' own needs matter, and nurses should share care to support them.

whyNot.0: This ignores his feeling of pressure.
whyNot.1: Sending him away is not what he asked for and may distress Aaron.
whyNot.2: Parents should not feel care is expected of them; it is their choice.

B.q: Evie, 7, has leukaemia. Her parents say her brother Sam, 5, has started wetting the bed and is clingy. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
options: Offer sibling support and involve Sam in age-appropriate ways
Advise that Sam should not visit to avoid upset
Reassure them this will settle when Evie goes home
Refer Sam to his GP for continence assessment
B.why: Illness affects the whole family; siblings may regress. Sibling support (for example from the play team) and appropriate involvement help Sam cope.

whyNot.1: Excluding siblings can increase anxiety; NG204 supports siblings being present if wished.
whyNot.3: Regression linked to family stress needs emotional support first rather than a continence referral.

C.q: Amina, 14, is admitted for investigations. Her parents ask that only female staff carry out intimate examinations, for religious reasons. Amina agrees. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain that staff are allocated by skill, not gender
Agree if a female doctor is on duty that day
Respect the request where possible and plan staffing
Ask Amina to decide without her parents present
C.why: NG204 supports cultural and religious beliefs; the request is reasonable, Amina agrees, and it can usually be planned for.

whyNot.0: Refusing without trying to accommodate does not respect the family's beliefs.
whyNot.1: Leaving it to chance is not planning care around the family's needs.
whyNot.3: Amina has already agreed; there is no conflict that requires separating her from her parents for this decision.

C.q: Leah, 9, has complex epilepsy and is ready for discharge after a long admission. Her parents care for her and two younger children. Which is the most family-centred discharge plan?
options: Discharge once the parents can give rescue medication
Plan training, respite and community support with them
Delay discharge until a full-time carer is funded
Ask the parents to manage and call if there are problems
C.why: Family-centred discharge considers the whole family: training, the parents' capacity with other children, respite and community services.

whyNot.0: Medication competence alone ignores the wider family needs.
whyNot.2: Delaying discharge is not in Leah's interests if support can be arranged.
whyNot.3: This leaves the family without planned support.

C.q: Tia, 4, is in the resuscitation room. Her mother wants to stay. The team is working effectively and there is space. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Ask her to wait outside until Tia is stable
Allow her to stay, without support, to avoid distraction
Allow her to stay once Tia has been intubated
Allow her to stay with a team member supporting her
C.why: RCUK 2025: allow parents to stay with the child if this does not compromise safety, and assign a dedicated team member to support and inform them.

whyNot.0: Parents should be allowed to stay where safe.
whyNot.1: A dedicated team member should support parents.
whyNot.2: There is no such condition; parents may stay throughout where it is safe.

reteach.title: Partners, not visitors
reteach.question: What changes when you see a parent as a partner rather than a visitor?

blocks.body: A visitor watches; a partner shares the plan. You ask what the family knows and wants, agree who does what, teach and supervise, and keep reviewing as the child's condition and the family's capacity change. The family's culture, faith and structure shape the plan.

blocks.text: Partnership is a choice for the family. Doing all the care must never be expected of parents.

explain.body: NG204: involve parents in discussions and decisions about babies and young children, recognising them as principal caregivers and advocates. Ask young people how involved they want their parents to be.

test.q: According to NICE NG204, how should parents of babies and young children be regarded?
options: As visitors with set visiting hours
As principal caregivers and advocates
As observers of nursing care
As the decision-makers for every age
test.why: NG204 1.5.1 recognises parents or carers as the principal caregivers and advocates of babies and young children.

whyNot.0: NG204 supports parents staying and flexible involvement.
whyNot.2: Parents can give developmentally appropriate care, not just observe.
whyNot.3: As children mature, their own role in decisions grows.

explain.body: Ask what the family wants to do, agree it, teach and supervise, record it and review. Parents' circumstances differ and should not be judged.

test.q: A mother wants to take over her son's NG feeds on the ward. What should the nurse do first?
options: Teach and supervise her until she is competent
Let her start straight away as she is his mother
Decline, as feeds are a nursing task
Ask the doctor to decide whether she may
test.why: Partnership includes teaching and supervising until the parent is confident and competent.

whyNot.1: Handing over without teaching risks harm.
whyNot.2: Parents can learn to give NG feeds with support.
whyNot.3: Agreeing parental participation is a nursing role with the family.

explain.body: Offer culturally and dietetically appropriate food choices, support prayer and religious practices, and let families know about chaplaincy and faith support (NG204 1.6.1, 1.9.9).

test.q: A family follows a halal diet. Which action best meets NG204?
options: Suggest the family bring all meals from home
Offer vegetarian options from the standard menu
Arrange halal meals as part of her menu choice
Advise that diet can wait until discharge
test.why: NG204 1.6.1: food choices should be culturally and dietetically appropriate at every meal.

whyNot.0: Families may bring food, but the hospital should provide appropriate options.
whyNot.1: Vegetarian food is not the same as meeting the family's halal needs.
whyNot.3: Nutrition supports recovery and should meet needs during admission.

explain.body: Use a professional interpreter when a parent or child has limited English. Children should not be used as interpreters except in an emergency; relatives may change or soften what is said.

test.q: Who should interpret when a parent speaks little English in a non-emergency?
options: A professional interpreter
The child's older sibling
A bilingual healthcare assistant
Another parent on the ward
test.why: A professional interpreter provides accurate, impartial and confidential interpreting.

whyNot.1: Children should not be used as interpreters outside an emergency.
whyNot.2: Staff who are not trained interpreters may be inaccurate and are not the standard.
whyNot.3: Another parent is untrained and breaches confidentiality.
